justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a baseline assumption of modest upward drift from what appears to be a current level around 415–416. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price, assuming mean-reversion tendencies dominate over very short windows and that no major scheduled catalysts were immediately imminent. The one-week estimate of 420 incorporates a slight positive bias consistent with the broader trend in equity markets, while acknowledging that short-term momentum can stall or reverse. The one-month estimate of 430 extends that gradual drift further, reflecting a compound of small expected gains rather than any specific fundamental catalyst — essentially a trend-following assumption applied conservatively.

The confidence interval widths expand as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, realized volatility in broad equity indices like the S&P 500 (which this appears to track, likely SPY or a similar instrument) tends to run around 0.8–1.2% on a typical session, giving a relatively tight band. By one week, you accumulate roughly the square root of five times that daily variance, and by one month the interval widens further to reflect not just price volatility but the possibility of regime changes in sentiment or macro conditions.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the downside, a sharper-than-expected Federal Reserve policy signal, a significant deterioration in labor market data, credit stress events, or geopolitical escalation could easily push prices below the lower bounds of my intervals. On the upside, a surprisingly dovish policy pivot, better-than-expected corporate earnings, or a resolution of macro uncertainty could drive a stronger rally than my intervals capture.

It is also worth noting that my intervals are calibrated for normal-to-moderately-stressed market conditions. Fat-tail events — a financial contagion episode, a sudden geopolitical shock, or a liquidity crisis — are structurally underweighted in any confidence interval built around historical volatility. The one-month interval in particular should be treated as indicative rather than precise, since a month is long enough for narratives to shift substantially in ways that simple volatility-scaling cannot fully anticipate.
